title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models

paper.title: Probabilistic Limit Order Book Forecasting with Conditional Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract. Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad , a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Limit order books (LOBs) are the main trading mechanism in modern electronic markets ( Gould et al., 2013 ) . A Level-2 LOB records the aggregate volume of outstanding buy and sell limit orders at each visible price level. The queue profile provides information about local liquidity, the supply of immediacy, and the short-horizon price impact faced by traders ( Bouchaud et al., 2018 ) . Accordingly, modeling LOB dynamics is central to tasks such as market forecasting, execution-strategy evaluation, and counterfactual market analysis ( Backhouse et al., 2025 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) have recently demonstrated strong empirical performance in time-series forecasting ( Rasul et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) and can learn highly complex distributions ( Chen et al., 2023b ; Yu and Yu, 2026 ) . These capabilities make DDPMs a natural choice for modeling limit order book dynamics ( Bouchaud et al., 2018 ; Backhouse et al., 2025 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Despite their empirical success, existing diffusion-based models of LOB snapshots typically do not explicitly employ a recurrent encoder of past LOB snapshots. Moreover, for the broader class of DDPMs with recurrent encoders, a general theoretical understanding of how conditioning on recurrently encoded histories affects predictive performance remains unexplored. In this work, we address both limitations by introducing LOBGrad , an encoder-conditioned DDPM for probabilistic LOB forecasting. Based on the TimeGrad framework ( Rasul et al., 2021 ) , LOBGrad integrates an autoregressive RNN encoder with a conditional diffusion-based generator. Specifically, the recurrent encoder maps past LOB snapshots to a lower-dimensional hidden state ( Schäfer and Zimmermann, 2007 ; Sirignano and Cont, 2019 ; Hanson and Raginsky, 2020 ) . This paper makes three contributions. (1) We adapt conditional diffusion forecasting to jointly predict queue depths and mid-price returns from recurrently encoded past LOB snapshots. (2) For the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective, we establish an excess-risk rate under the stated mixing and regularity assumptions. Under a contractive hidden-state recurrence, the dimension appearing in the encoder-approximation rate is the hidden-state dimension m m rather than the flattened conditioning-window dimension s ​ d y sd_{y} . (3) We show that LOBGrad outperforms baseline models on LOB-Bench-inspired distributional metrics ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) using Bitcoin data and U.S. equity data for Alphabet and Meta, and reproduces key microstructure stylized facts. We additionally demonstrate the practical utility of accurately forecasting LOB dynamics in a downstream execution task. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the LOB representation and our model architecture. Section 4 presents the theoretical results. Section 5 reports the experimental evaluation. Section 6 concludes the paper.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: LOBGrad models the conditional distribution over future LOB states and can generate multiple plausible trajectories. This objective differs from classification-based or point-forecasting methods ( Prata et al., 2024 ) . Our work extends the literature in the following two respects.

sections.heading: Generative models for LOB dynamics.
sections.text: A growing body of work uses generative models to capture LOB dynamics. Early approaches employ GANs to generate order streams and learn conditional distributions of future LOB snapshots ( Coletta et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2020 ) . Notably, ( Cont et al., 2023 ) propose a Wasserstein GAN that conditions on the current LOB snapshot and models the transition between consecutive LOB snapshots. Recent work has moved beyond GANs. ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) uses a token-level autoregressive S5 model to generate message streams for a LOB simulator, while ( Berti et al., 2025 ) introduces TRADES, a Transformer-based conditional diffusion model that generates individual orders conditioned on recent order flow. At the snapshot level, ( Backhouse et al., 2025 ) represents LOB snapshots as images and apply image-based diffusion. DiffLOB ( Wang and Ventre, 2026 ) models future LOB trajectories conditional on the observed history and market-regime variables describing trend, volatility, liquidity, and order-flow imbalance. Its conditioning setup is closely related to that of our no-encoder ablation. Despite their empirical success, none of these diffusion-based snapshot models employs an autoregressive recurrent encoder. Their conditioning relies on the current LOB snapshot, image-based spatial structure, or regime-level information rather than on a learned recurrent summary of the past LOB snapshots.

sections.heading: Theory for diffusion models.
sections.text: Statistical theory for diffusion models has established approximation, estimation, and sampling guarantees, mainly for unconditional distribution learning ( Chen et al., 2023a ; Oko et al., 2023 ; Benton et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Li and Yan, 2025 ) . Recent work also studies conditional diffusion models, including classifier-free guidance and conditional distribution estimation with observed covariates ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . These results typically assume independent samples and use feedforward networks conditioned on fixed covariates. Thus, they do not directly apply to our setting, where the conditioning variables are learned recurrent summaries of overlapping windows from a dependent time series. We address this problem by bounding the excess risk of the one-step DDPM ε \varepsilon -prediction objective under exponential mixing.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate LOBGrad on three Level-2 LOB datasets: BTC/USDT from Binance and GOOGL and META from Databento. We focus on BTC/USDT, as Bitcoin is a highly liquid cryptocurrency, and its continuous trading provides a dense high-frequency sample without scheduled overnight closures. In this section, we provide the most detailed analysis for BTC/USDT and additional results for GOOGL and META to assess whether the results extend to U.S. equities. The BTC/USDT dataset consists of snapshots collected at 5-second intervals from the Binance public REST endpoint between October 1 and October 21, 2023. It contains 308,826 snapshots and is split chronologically into 15 training days, 2 validation days, and 4 test days. We aggregate the first 100 raw price levels into d = 5 d=5 bins per side using a grid width of δ = 2 \delta=2 USDT, giving d y = 2 ​ d + 1 = 11 d_{y}=2d+1=11 in ( 1 ). This choice of d d and δ \delta covers approximately 98% of the observed mid-price changes between consecutive snapshots. The GOOGL and META datasets use Databento’s MBP-10 schema and cover July 1--23, 2026. We retain the same model architecture and hyperparameters across all three datasets and refit the model separately on each dataset 1 1 1 The code is available at https://github.com/junyuchen-econ/LOBGrad . .

sections.heading: Ablations and baselines.
sections.text: We compare LOBGrad against three ablations (LG-Q, LG-R, and LG-NE), four external baselines (CGAN, PTM, TransLOB, and DeepLOB), and two classical statistical models (Hawkes and Poisson). LG-Q and LG-R use queue-only and return-only targets, respectively, while LG-NE removes the recurrent encoder and conditions on the flattened history of dimension s ​ d y = 1100 sd_{y}=1100 , isolating the effect of recurrent summarization. The external baselines are a conditional Wasserstein GAN (CGAN) ( Cont et al., 2023 ) ; PTM, our re-implementation of the image-format snapshot diffusion model proposed by Backhouse et al. (2025) , for which public code is unavailable; TransLOB ( Wallbridge, 2020 ) , a transformer-based model; and DeepLOB ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) . We adapt TransLOB and DeepLOB from their original classification setting ( Prata et al., 2024 ) to our probabilistic forecasting framework.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: Hyperparameters for LOBGrad and the learnable baselines are selected on the validation split using the Optuna Python package with median pruning. The selected model uses a look-back length of s = 100 s=100 , a one-layer LSTM with hidden size m = 151 m=151 , a 255 255 -unit noise MLP, and a 32 32 -dimensional diffusion-step embedding. We use K = 102 K=102 diffusion steps with a linear schedule from β 1 = 10 − 4 \beta_{1}=10^{-4} to β K = 0.1 \beta_{K}=0.1 . The model is trained with the Huber noise-prediction loss using Adam. The empirical study covers three components: distributional generation quality evaluated on 500 held-out windows with 100-step contexts, 20-step forecast horizons, and 100 autoregressive rollouts per window; an analysis of return stylized facts; and a downstream limit-order execution task. The models are trained on a single NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU. LOBGrad has 248,181 parameters and generates 100 paths at one-step and 20-step forecast horizons in 0.038 and 0.37 seconds, respectively, on a single Apple M4 CPU. Both runtimes are below the 5-second snapshot interval, allowing forecasts to be regenerated at every snapshot without dedicated hardware.

sections.text: Figure 4 evaluates whether LOBGrad reproduces standard stylized facts of price series on BTC/USDT. We compare real and generated successive-snapshot mid-price changes using the marginal return distribution, the return ACF, and the absolute-return ACF. Generated samples are obtained from 100 autoregressive rollouts for each of the 500 evaluation windows. LOBGrad closely matches the empirical return distribution, captures the small first-lag autocorrelation in returns, and partially recovers the short-horizon dependence in absolute returns. sections.heading: 5.3. Downstream Task
sections.text: Beyond distributional metrics, we test whether forecasts can be used for execution decisions. We consider a stylized single-shot sell problem. At the start of each test window, an agent must sell a quantity Q Q of BTC. The order size Q Q is fixed across windows within a run and is twice the training-set mean cumulative bid depth over the first three grid bins. The action j = − 1 j=-1 denotes an immediate market sell, while j ≥ 0 j\geq 0 posts a passive sell limit order at p lim = p mid ​ ( 0 ) + j ​ δ p_{\mathrm{lim}}=p_{\mathrm{mid}}(0)+j\delta , where δ = 2 \delta=2 USDT, p mid ​ ( 0 ) p_{\mathrm{mid}}(0) is the mid-price at order arrival, and waits up to 20 future snapshots. We take the offset as j ∈ { − 1 , 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 } j\in\{-1,0,1,2,3\} . The order is treated as passively filled if the mid-price reaches the limit price or if the queue at the corresponding ask level is sufficiently depleted. Otherwise, it is executed at the final snapshot by walking the bid book. sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we introduce LOBGrad, an encoder-conditioned DDPM that combines an autoregressive recurrent encoder with a conditional noise-prediction network for probabilistic LOB forecasting. Across BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META, LOBGrad improves distributional forecasting performance, reproduces key microstructure stylized facts, and provides practical value in a downstream execution task. The theoretical analysis provides a one-step excess-risk bound for a recurrently conditioned DDPM under the stated mixing, smoothness, and network-class assumptions. This result motivates recurrent conditioning: under a stable contractive latent-state dynamics, the encoder approximation error term depends on the hidden-state dimension m m rather than the flattened history dimension s ​ d y sd_{y} . Future work will extend these guarantees to multi-step autoregressive forecasts and investigate recurrently conditioned diffusion models across broader market settings.

Modeling limit order book (LOB) dynamics is central to market forecasting and execution-strategy evaluation. While diffusion models achieve strong empirical performance, existing LOB snapshot models typically lack a learned recurrent encoder and formal statistical guarantees. We introduce LOBGrad , a conditional DDPM framework for probabilistic LOB forecasting that combines an autoregressive RNN encoder with a diffusion-based generator. In particular, we establish an excess-risk oracle inequality for the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective under exponential mixing and regularity assumptions. We further show that, under contractive dynamics, the dependence on the conditioning-window length can be reduced to a dependence on the latent-state dimension. Experiments on BTC/USDT, GOOGL, and META show that LOBGrad improves on its encoder-free diffusion ablation across all reported queue metrics and obtains competitive results against other baselines. It also reproduces the key stylized facts of LOB microstructure, and yields reasonably calibrated queue-based predictive intervals. A stylized downstream task illustrates the potential value of the generated forecasts. Introduction Limit order books (LOBs) are the main trading mechanism in modern electronic markets ( Gould et al., 2013 ) . A Level-2 LOB records the aggregate volume of outstanding buy and sell limit orders at each visible price level. The queue profile provides information about local liquidity, the supply of immediacy, and the short-horizon price impact faced by traders ( Bouchaud et al., 2018 ) . Accordingly, modeling LOB dynamics is central to tasks such as market forecasting, execution-strategy evaluation, and counterfactual market analysis ( Backhouse et al., 2025 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) have recently demonstrated strong empirical performance in time-series forecasting ( Rasul et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) and can learn highly complex distributions ( Chen et al., 2023b ; Yu and Yu, 2026 ) . These capabilities make DDPMs a natural choice for modeling limit order book dynamics ( Bouchaud et al., 2018 ; Backhouse et al., 2025 ; Wang and Ventre, 2025 ) . Despite their empirical success, existing diffusion-based models of LOB snapshots typically do not explicitly employ a recurrent encoder of past LOB snapshots. Moreover, for the broader class of DDPMs with recurrent encoders, a general theoretical understanding of how conditioning on recurrently encoded histories affects predictive performance remains unexplored. In this work, we address both limitations by introducing LOBGrad , an encoder-conditioned DDPM for probabilistic LOB forecasting. Based on the TimeGrad framework ( Rasul et al., 2021 ) , LOBGrad integrates an autoregressive RNN encoder with a conditional diffusion-based generator. Specifically, the recurrent encoder maps past LOB snapshots to a lower-dimensional hidden state ( Schäfer and Zimmermann, 2007 ; Sirignano and Cont, 2019 ; Hanson and Raginsky, 2020 ) . This paper makes three contributions. (1) We adapt conditional diffusion forecasting to jointly predict queue depths and mid-price returns from recurrently encoded past LOB snapshots. (2) For the one-step DDPM noise-prediction objective, we establish an excess-risk rate under the stated mixing and regularity assumptions. Under a contractive hidden-state recurrence, the dimension appearing in the encoder-approximation rate is the hidden-state dimension m m rather than the flattened conditioning-window dimension s ​ d y sd_{y} . (3) We show that LOBGrad outperforms baseline models on LOB-Bench-inspired distributional metrics ( Nagy et al., 2025 ) using Bitcoin data and U.S. equity data for Alphabet and Meta, and reproduces key microstructure stylized facts. We additionally demonstrate the practical utility of accurately forecasting LOB dynamics in a downstream execution task. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 introduces the LOB representation and our model architecture. Section 4 presents the theoretical results. Section 5 reports the experimental evaluation. Section 6 concludes the paper. 2. Related Work LOBGrad models the conditional distribution over future LOB states and can generate multiple plausible trajectories. This objective differs from classification-based or point-forecasting methods ( Prata et al., 2024 ) . Our work extends the literature in the following two respects. Generative models for LOB dynamics. A growing body of work uses generative models to capture LOB dynamics. Early approaches employ GANs to generate order streams and learn conditional distributions of future LOB snapshots ( Coletta et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2020 ) . Notably, ( Cont et al., 2023 ) propose a Wasserstein GAN that conditions on the current LOB snapshot and models the transition between consecutive LOB snapshots. Recent work has moved beyond GANs. ( Nagy et al., 2023 ) uses a token-level autoregressive S5 model to generate message streams for a LOB simulator, while ( Berti et al., 2025 ) introduces TRADES, a Transformer-based conditional diffusion model that generates individual orders conditioned on recent order flow. At the snapshot level, ( Backhouse et al., 2025 ) represents LOB snapshots as images and apply image-based diffusion. DiffLOB ( Wang and Ventre, 2026 ) models future LOB trajectories conditional on the observed history and market-regime variables describing trend, volatility, liquidity, and order-flow imbalance. Its conditioning setup is closely related to that of our no-encoder ablation. Despite their empirical success, none of these diffusion-based snapshot models employs an autoregressive recurrent encoder. Their conditioning relies on the current LOB snapshot, image-based spatial structure, or regime-level information rather than on a learned recurrent summary of the past LOB snapshots. Theory for diffusion models. Statistical theory for diffusion models has established approximation, estimation, and sampling guarantees, mainly for unconditional distribution learning ( Chen et al., 2023a ; Oko et al., 2023 ; Benton et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Li and Yan, 2025 ) . Recent work also studies conditional diffusion models, including classifier-free guidance and conditional distribution estimation with observed covariates ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . These results typically assume independent samples and use feedforward networks conditioned on fixed covariates. Thus, they do not directly apply to our setting, where the conditioning variables are learned recurrent summaries of overlapping windows from a dependent time series. We address this problem by bounding the excess risk of the one-step DDPM ε \varepsilon -prediction objective under exponential mixing. 3. We evaluate LOBGrad on three Level-2 LOB datasets: BTC/USDT from Binance and GOOGL and META from Databento. We focus on BTC/USDT, as Bitcoin is a highly liquid cryptocurrency, and its continuous trading provides a dense high-frequency sample without scheduled overnight closures. In this section, we provide the most detailed analysis for BTC/USDT and additional results for GOOGL and META to assess whether the results extend to U.S. equities. The BTC/USDT dataset consists of snapshots collected at 5-second intervals from the Binance public REST endpoint between October 1 and October 21, 2023. It contains 308,826 snapshots and is split chronologically into 15 training days, 2 validation days, and 4 test days. We aggregate the first 100 raw price levels into d = 5 d=5 bins per side using a grid width of δ = 2 \delta=2 USDT, giving d y = 2 ​ d + 1 = 11 d_{y}=2d+1=11 in ( 1 ). This choice of d d and δ \delta covers approximately 98% of the observed mid-price changes between consecutive snapshots. The GOOGL and META datasets use Databento’s MBP-10 schema and cover July 1--23, 2026. Ablations and baselines. We compare LOBGrad against three ablations (LG-Q, LG-R, and LG-NE), four external baselines (CGAN, PTM, TransLOB, and DeepLOB), and two classical statistical models (Hawkes and Poisson). LG-Q and LG-R use queue-only and return-only targets, respectively, while LG-NE removes the recurrent encoder and conditions on the flattened history of dimension s ​ d y = 1100 sd_{y}=1100 , isolating the effect of recurrent summarization. The external baselines are a conditional Wasserstein GAN (CGAN) ( Cont et al., 2023 ) ; PTM, our re-implementation of the image-format snapshot diffusion model proposed by Backhouse et al. (2025) , for which public code is unavailable; TransLOB ( Wallbridge, 2020 ) , a transformer-based model; and DeepLOB ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) . We adapt TransLOB and DeepLOB from their original classification setting ( Prata et al., 2024 ) to our probabilistic forecasting framework. Experimental setup. Hyperparameters for LOBGrad and the learnable baselines are selected on the validation split using the Optuna Python package with median pruning. The selected model uses a look-back length of s = 100 s=100 , a one-layer LSTM with hidden size m = 151 m=151 , a 255 255 -unit noise MLP, and a 32 32 -dimensional diffusion-step embedding. We use K = 102 K=102 diffusion steps with a linear schedule from β 1 = 10 − 4 \beta_{1}=10^{-4} to β K = 0.1 \beta_{K}=0.1 . The model is trained with the Huber noise-prediction loss using Adam. The empirical study covers three components: distributional generation quality evaluated on 500 held-out windows with 100-step contexts, 20-step forecast horizons, and 100 autoregressive rollouts per window; an analysis of return stylized facts; and a downstream limit-order execution task. The models are trained on a single NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU. LOBGrad has 248,181 parameters and generates 100 paths at one-step and 20-step forecast horizons in 0.038 and 0.37 seconds, respectively, on a single Apple M4 CPU.
